Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

issues.item: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: This avoidance item is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For toxic chemical exposure, the reported triggers, threat beliefs, and memory problems center on unpredictability, loud sounds, incomprehensible chatter, and difficulty verbalising the event. Avoidance of military or police uniforms/weapons implies a different threat context involving armed authority or assault, and there are no corresponding trigger, threat, or memory items linking the trauma to uniforms, weapons, or law-enforcement cues. This creates a clinically implausible mismatch within the five components.

vignette: When the municipal ventilation system failed, a cloud of pale, acrid vapor seeped through the third-floor records office where Sylvia worked as a civil servant. Alarms blared, and supervisors barked overlapping, incomprehensible chatter as they scrambled to coordinate an evacuation. Sylvia clutched her desk, her lungs burning, watching strangers in protective gear move with frantic, unpredictable urgency. She tried to mentally catalogue what was happening, but her mind went blank, leaving only a heavy, nonverbal knot in her chest. The incident's fragmented quality made it impossible for her to piece together a coherent account, and whenever she tried to deliberately recall the morning, her access to the memory vanished entirely. The very unpredictability of the evacuation, the confusing radio instructions, and the pressure to process what was happening all forged a potent association that would later dictate her daily life. In the weeks that followed, that memory gap bred a new pattern of control. Because she could not explain clearly what had happened to her husband or her colleagues, she stopped attempting to talk about it, which directly led her to rehearse every interaction in advance. This rigid preparation became necessary precisely because unpredictable situations at work-shift changes, surprise audits, sudden building repairs-sparked immediate dread, pulling her back into the original moment. Encountering those unpredictable routines or incomprehensible chatter jolted her into high alert, making ordinary municipal hallways feel as dangerous as the compromised ventilation shaft. Discussing the facility's safety protocols or facing unexpected audits made her lose her thread, which then triggered fresh panic. Her reliance on rehearsing conversations and avoiding physical contact only widened the gap between her and the world, making every shift change and overlapping office murmur feel inherently unpredictable. That fragmented recall made unpredictable situations at work feel inherently destabilizing, which then triggered fresh panic. Her inability to access the memory deliberately only fed the cycle, transforming colleagues' questions into sudden, felt threats. Being confined to a safe zone meant any unexpected sound jolted her into high alert, which in turn made deliberately recalling the event impossible. Because she was constantly scanning for threat, strangers approaching her desk felt predatory, which in turn made unpredictable routines feel even more destabilizing. This avoidance of hospitals and physical examinations reinforced her conviction that the world itself was dangerous, ensuring that strangers and loud noises remained perpetual threats. Now, at fifty-one, Sylvia still sits at her civil service desk, her posture rigid, her phone screen darkened to avoid unexpected calls. She avoids being touched even when her husband reaches for her shoulder, flinching as if expecting another cloud to materialize. The concrete consequence of this narrowing world is visible in her work: she has been sidelined from inter-departmental meetings, her promotions stalled, and her marriage strained by her insistence on sleeping in her own bed and refusing to leave the apartment for grocery runs. What finally brought her into my office was a panic attack during a routine permit review, where the murmur of a nearby phone conversation became completely incomprehensible chatter that made her heart hammer against her ribs. She came hoping to understand why her own mind feels like a locked room, afraid that if she ever speaks the event aloud, she will never feel safe in any place again.
